sections.html:
• Common name: Red Devil Crab (also Red Vampire Crab)
  • Type: semi-terrestrial crab
  • Minimum tank: 20 litres
  • Keeping: easy; breeding: easy to medium
  • Carapace size: up to 2.5 cm; leg span up to 5–7 cm
  • Aquarium type: paludarium (both land and freshwater areas)
  • Humidity: 75% and higher
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: mostly carnivore
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Life span: up to 2 years
  • Colour: orange or red with yellow eyes

There is not much information on their natural distribution. So far, these crabs are known to be endemic to an island in Central Java, Indonesia.

The species was named after the Rolf C. Hagen Group of Companies, a major pet supplies company, which supported the study in Java. The common name "Red Devil Crab" was chosen as a marketing move and as part of a theme: Geosesarma dennerle (Vampire crab) and Geosesarma hagen share the same natural habitat.

Geosesarma hagen lives in forests (between rocks and among dense vegetation) near freshwater rivers and lakes. It does not depend on saltwater for development.

In nature, adult crabs are not found in the water very often and mostly live on moist banks. Juveniles are often in the water or very close to the waterline, and are not frequently seen on the drier forest ground.

Red Devil crabs require less space than other crustaceans. A 20-litre tank with lots of hiding places can easily house 3 crabs (1 male and 2 females). This applies to most Geosesarma species (Vampire crabs, Tangerine-head crabs, etc.).

Some articles give a minimum of 40 litres or more. A bigger tank makes it easier to set up a paludarium with diverse areas, but as a minimum acceptable requirement it is all about hiding places: in a 40-litre tank you will rarely see these small crabs unless you keep at least 7–8 of them.

Red Devil crabs are great escape artists, so a tight-fitting lid is essential.

Land vs water ratio

Red Devil crabs are semi-terrestrial, not aquatic. Ideally the land area should take at least 70% of the space in the tank, or more. Juveniles molt frequently and need water for it, and water provides more hiding places and a safer environment.

Water bowl

Red Devil crabs do not need a lot of water, so instead of a complex setup with filters you can use a simple water bowl, following these rules:

  • The bowl should be deep enough to completely submerge the crabs; 5–7 cm is enough.
  • It should be big enough to fit at least half of the crabs at the same time. For 5 adult crabs, the bowl should fit at least 3 at once, so at least 15 × 15 cm.
  • It should have some hiding places, because the crabs molt in the water.

Red Devil crabs cannot stay in the water all the time and will drown, so provide a variety of surfaces to get out of the water.

Pros of water bowls: water changes are very easy, and no filter is needed to keep the water clean. Cons: bowls usually do not look great unless decorated and hidden well, and the water must be replaced every 2–3 days.

Substrate

Use coconut fiber, soil and peat. A deep substrate is not needed; 7–10 cm is usually enough. It lets the crabs dig their own dens and helps maintain humidity. The substrate should always be moist, with a "sandcastle" consistency: it holds its shape when squeezed but does not drip or pool water. To test it, push a pencil all the way down and pull it back up: the tunnel should not collapse.

Humidity

Red Devil crabs need moist, humid air to breathe. Humidity should be more than 70%, ideally 75–90%. It can be changed by adding moisture or by reducing or increasing ventilation; expect some trial and error. Stability and high humidity are among the reasons people fail to keep them.

Decorations and hiding spots

They need a lot of hiding places, even in the water. The more hiding places, the more active the crabs become, because they feel more secure. Live plants, PVC pipes, pieces of bark, driftwood, wood, stones, nets and porous bricks give shelter. Moss is a favourite place to sit and hide.

Molting

To grow, the crab sheds its exoskeleton in a process called molting, which also lets it restore lost limbs. It has 4 phases: pre-molt, molt, post-molt and inter-molt.

  • Never disturb crabs that are molting; it is the most stressful moment of their life.
  • Keep giving calcium-rich and mineral-rich foods so the shell hardens faster.
  • Do not remove old exoskeletons; they contain many nutrients and the crab will eat them later.
  • Keep putting in new food even if the crabs are missing for days.
  • Do not panic if they do not come out for a few days after molting.

Handling

  • They are not pets to play with; do not take them out without need.
  • Never lift them by the legs or claws; they can lose a limb by autotomy.
  • Do not leave uneaten food too long, as it causes smell and bacteria. Crabs can store uneaten food in their burrows.
  • Keep the lid tightly closed.

Red Devil crabs need freshwater only. In a classic paludarium they thrive in:

  • pH: at least 7.0–8.0; if the pH is too low they may become lethargic.
  • Temperature: 24–28°C.
  • Hardness: KH 0–10 and GH 4–16.

If you use tap water, add a water conditioner to remove chlorine and chloramine. If you use RO/DI water, you must remineralise it.

Crabs are cold-blooded: their metabolism slows when the temperature drops, and if it drops too low or too fast it can cause temperature shock. A heat mat under the tank can help keep it warm.

No special lighting is required, as Red Devil crabs are nocturnal. If you have plants, adapt the lighting to their needs; otherwise you may not need any. A heat mat under the tank can keep it warm, and a tight-fitting lid is essential.

Although in captivity these crabs can eat detritus and dead plant parts, they are not vegetarians. According to studies, they seem to be more carnivorous, feeding at least partially on insects living on the ground. They accept a variety of foods but are much more vigorous when hunting live prey (woodlice, worms, fruit flies, small crickets, bugs).

Foods they will enjoy: shrimp pellets, shrimp granules, fish food (flakes), shrimp food, frozen bloodworms, detritus worms and brine shrimp.

They need a balanced diet and should not be given the same food every day, which can make them sick and shorten their lifespan:

  • Protein (the main part)
  • Vegetables and fruits (broccoli, cabbage, carrots, cucumber, lettuce, corn, spinach, peas, squash, leafy greens; apple, banana, pear, melon, mango) and leaves
  • Calcium

Calcium is a crucial component of the shell, cellular function and overall health. A deficiency can cause weakness and cracks in the shell, making the crab susceptible to disease, heat and dehydration. Sources include kale, broccoli, spinach, cuttlebones, eggshells, figs, nuts, oyster shells, seaweed, seeds and insects. A few small pieces of cuttlebone should be in the tank all the time.

Feeding frequency

Adults can be fed 3–4 times a week, while juveniles should be fed daily. Do not let the crabs starve, or despite their relatively peaceful temper they may even cannibalise each other. Food can be left for 24 hours before removal to prevent mould. It is best to feed in the evening or at night, as they are nocturnal.

Colour

As with shrimp, adding astaxanthin to the diet can enhance their coloration.

Plant safety

Red Devil crabs are plant safe: they are mostly carnivorous, do not eat live plants and usually do not uproot or cut them.

Red Devil crabs are hunters: woodlice, worms, fruit flies and other live foods are their preference. They are nocturnal and spend most of the day hidden from the light; at night they roam both on land and underwater looking for food or a new hiding spot. Once settled they become more outgoing and come out more often, even in the daytime.

They are active and social, preferring the company of their own species. Larger colonies often have more active members. They are not territorial or aggressive, but like most crabs there can be occasional fights, which is why hiding places are so important.

They are not true diggers, but can push out some soil to make their own dens, usually at the edge of the water in nature.

Once settled and acclimatised they become quite hardy. Poor handling during capture and shipment means they may die soon after purchase, which is why some hobbyists consider them not beginner-friendly.

Tank mates

The ideal situation is a species tank, with one male and multiple females. Although G. hagen is probably one of the most social crabs in the genus, in large groups they compete for food (which can cause aggression), so keep them well fed, and the tank needs lots of hiding places.

In a paludarium it is possible to keep dwarf shrimp and small fish with them, as adults spend little time in the water.

Bad tank mates: larger or aggressive fish, any crayfish, other crab species and dwarf frogs. Keeping them with other Geosesarma (Tangerine-head crabs, Vampire crabs) or Metasesarma (Marble crabs, Red Apple crabs) is possible but not recommended, as some species are more aggressive or smaller, which can cause conflicts.

Geosesarma hagen is sexually dimorphic.

  • Abdomen: males have a narrow, slimmer plate while females have a broad plate on the belly. Females may also carry fertilised eggs.
  • Claws: males have larger and sometimes brighter claws; females have claws about half that size.

Size is not a reliable way to sex them: unlike most crabs, where males are bigger, in the genus Geosesarma it is hard to tell because of their small size.

If a female is ready to mate, she allows a male to approach; the male flips her upside down and wraps himself around her to fertilise. Mating usually lasts several minutes.

Red Devil crabs breed well once old enough and established in the tank. Reproduction has not been described in the scientific literature, but there are reports of successful captive breeding:

  • They do not need saltwater to breed; females release eggs in freshwater.
  • Female size correlates with the number of eggs; each female carries a few dozen eggs.
  • Incubation lasts 30–50 days depending on temperature.
  • Before hatching, females become more secretive and hide almost all the time.
  • The eggs are large with direct development (no larval stages). Females release tiny copies of the adults (1–2 mm).
  • Young are completely dark, without orange or red colour, and spend most of their time in the water, using it for protection more than older crabs.
  • Small crabs should be fed every day with the same food as adults; just crush the pellets.

Adults usually do not cannibalise young if they are not hungry, but keeping them in the same tank is not recommended. The young are so tiny and secretive that they are often not found until they grow bigger; moving a berried female to a rearing tank is the only solution suggested.

Appearance: like all crabs they have ten legs including two pincers used for eating; the claws are small and do not open very wide. The body is squarish and slightly wider than long. The anterior part of the carapace and the walking legs are dark brown, the posterior part of the carapace is orange or reddish, the abdomen is greyish, the eyes are bright yellow and the claws are orange or reddish. Hatchlings are almost dark, while young crabs are generally more reddish than orange.

Lifespan: under optimal conditions up to 2 years, with an average of around 1.5 years, depending on disease, poor living conditions and shipment stress.
